extracted.intended_audience: general readers, hobbyists, telegraphists, and early electrical experimenters interested in building and understanding telephones
extracted.subtask_description: Practical instructions and operational guidance for constructing and using a basic Bell-style telephone (diaphragm, magnet, spool, wiring) and for understanding its performance limits and interference issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diaphragm specification and mounting
rubrics_metrics.description: The diaphragm is a thin, circular sheet of iron, a couple of inches in diameter, held by its rim with its centre very close to the end of the magnetized bar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The diaphragm (vibrator) must be thin and mounted so air-wave vibrations throw it into motion; its least polished side should face the magnet and the part opposite the magnet can be scraped to expose iron. Proper mounting ensures the diaphragm reproduces the complex wave-systems of voice and music.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnet specification and adjustment
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a strongly-magnetized steel rod about four inches long and three-eighths of an inch in diameter; its distance from the diaphragm is adjusted by a screw.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Magnet strength and adjustable spacing are critical: the magnet must be close enough to the diaphragm to respond to its vibrations but adjustable to tune the instrument's sensitivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spool winding and wire gauge
rubrics_metrics.description: Make a spool about one inch long and wind it with about fifty yards of No. 36 or 38 silk-covered copper wire (thickness of a bristle).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the specified thin, silk-covered wire and the recommended winding length to produce the delicate magnetic currents required for telephonic operation. Join spool ends to the line-wires.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mouth-piece size and placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a movable wooden mouth-piece with an opening at the bottom about the size of a dime that reaches to within about one-eighth of an inch of the diaphragm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concentrating the voice on a narrow space at the middle of the diaphragm improves transmission; the mouth-piece should fit neatly and be positioned to focus sound precisely on the diaphragm centre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instrument assembly and materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct the body from thin sheet-brass (tube 1 in. long, 2 in. diameter with 1/2 in. flange), use a ferrotype-plate for the diaphragm, cut wooden washers and brass spool parts to fit, and screw parts firmly through the flanges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Careful fitting of parts (tube, flange, washer, spool, magnet) and attention to which face of the plate is exposed to the magnet are necessary for reliable operation; the diaphragm's least polished side should face the magnet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Line connection and station configuration
rubrics_metrics.description: Join the ends of the spool-wire to the line-wires that run to another similar instrument; stations may use two telephones so one is held to the ear while the other is used for sending.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple telephones can be connected in an office so several persons may listen simultaneously; wiring must be correctly joined and routed to the remote instrument(s).

rubrics_metrics.name: Operating posture and speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Hold the instrument to the mouth and speak distinctly in ordinary tones or even a whisper; then hold the instrument to the ear to receive the answer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Articulation and volume affect intelligibility—speaking clearly and using the mouth-piece correctly are important. For noisy environments or long messages, use two instruments at each station so one may be held to the ear continuously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance limits by line resistance (distance guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: With artificial resistance: ~1,000 ohms (≈70 miles) yields perfect but not very loud sound; ≈4,000 ohms (≈300 miles) still allows articulation; ≈10,000 ohms (≈700 miles) transmits tone but not articulate speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These resistance-to-distance observations indicate practical range limits; beyond certain resistance the telephone transmits tone and inflection but loses word articulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for a 'silent line' and induction avoidance
rubrics_metrics.description: The telephone works with very delicate magnetic currents and requires a 'silent line' because induction from stronger nearby currents (telegraph Morse, ABC/printer, transmitters) can set up opposing currents and overpower telephone signals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid routing telephone wires near wires carrying strong currents, minimize proximity to active telegraph instruments, ensure good insulation, and reduce sources of induction to prevent the pot-boiling-like noise and modulation by other instruments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensitivity to ambient and mechanical noise
rubrics_metrics.description: Ambient noises (e.g., heavy lorry rumbling, office machinery) can drown faint telephone signals—silence in the room is necessary for distinguishing articulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a quiet environment during telephonic communication; otherwise, only tone or inflection may be perceivable when background noise is present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symmetric two-end arrangement (bidirectional operation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The arrangement being the same at each end, the machine works both ways so that vibrations at one diaphragm produce corresponding vibrations at the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct both ends with the same components and adjustments so each instrument can act as sender and receiver; this symmetry enables conversation as if parties were in the same room.
